research.dimension: Claude (Anthropic) API costs and whether a Claude subscription includes API credits (checked 2026-10-30)

items.claim: The Pro plan does not include any Claude API / Console usage. API usage has to be paid separately through a Console account.
items.value: Pro: no API credits included
items.short_quote: The Pro plan does not include API usage through the Claude Console.

items.claim: Claude paid plans and the Claude Console are separate products, and the API is billed separately from the subscription. The article now carves out Max and Team, which include monthly API credits.
items.value: API billed separately; exception: Max and Team include monthly API credits
items.short_quote: the Claude API is billed separately
items.caveats: The article says Max and Team include monthly credits for the Claude API (see sub-03).

items.topic: Monthly API credits included in subscriptions
items.claim: Monthly API credits come only with Max 5x, Max 20x and Team plans (discounted Team plans included). Free, Pro and Enterprise are not eligible.
items.value: Eligible: Max 5x, Max 20x, Team. Not eligible: Free, Pro, Enterprise
items.short_quote: Free, Pro, and Enterprise plans aren't eligible.
items.caveats: Announced in an October 7, 2026 update (see sub-14). Which plan the user is on is unknown, so whether he gets credits is still unconfirmed.

items.topic: Monthly API credits included in subscriptions
items.claim: Monthly API credit amounts per plan. Team credits are pooled across seats and capped at $500 per month.
items.value: Max 5x: $100 USD/month; Max 20x: $200 USD/month; Team: $20 USD per Standard seat and $100 USD per Premium seat, pooled, cap $500 USD/month
items.short_quote: capped at $500 USD
items.caveats: Amounts are in USD. Example from the page: 3 Standard + 2 Premium seats = $260/month.

items.topic: Monthly API credits: eligibility and claiming
items.claim: To claim the credits, the subscription must be active and in good standing and must have been on an eligible plan for 7 days. The claimer must be the Max subscriber (or a Team Owner/Primary Owner) and hold the Owner, Admin or Billing role in the Console org. Claiming is done on claude.ai in a web browser (Settings > Billing > API credits > Link organization). No payment method is needed on the Claude Platform.
items.value: 7-day wait; claim on claude.ai web; no card needed
items.short_quote: No payment method needed.
items.caveats: Only one Console organization can be linked, and the user cannot change the link himself (support has to). Linking requires accepting the Supplemental Credit Terms.

items.claim: The credits cover the Claude API (Messages API and Message Batches API), the Console Playground, Claude Managed Agents, and the Claude Agent SDK / claude -p when run with an API key from the linked org. They do not cover interactive Claude Code, extra usage in the Claude apps, or Bedrock/Vertex/Foundry.
items.value: Covers Messages + Batches API, Playground, Managed Agents, Agent SDK (API key); excludes interactive Claude Code, extra usage, cloud platforms
items.short_quote: The Claude API (Messages API and Message Batches API)
items.caveats: The article says nothing explicit about server tools such as web search. Since they are billed as Claude API usage they are presumably covered, but that is not stated.

items.topic: Monthly API credits: expiry and order
items.claim: Included credits refresh each billing cycle (monthly on annual plans) and do not roll over. They are spent before any purchased credits.
items.value: Expire at the end of each billing cycle; no rollover; used first
items.short_quote: Doesn't roll over. Unused credits expire at the end of each billing cycle.
items.caveats: Auto-reload is based only on the purchased balance (per the platform docs page).

items.claim: If the linked org has no other credits, API requests stop until the next monthly credits arrive. Usage is never charged to the Claude subscription. To keep going, the user must buy credits or turn on auto-reload in the Console.
items.value: Hard stop when credits run out (unless purchased credits or auto-reload exist)
items.short_quote: Usage is never charged to your Claude plan.
items.caveats: This acts as a natural hard budget cap for a pipeline that runs only on included credits.

items.topic: Monthly API credits: tiers and spend caps
items.claim: Usage paid with included credits still counts toward the org's monthly spend cap. Orgs linked to an eligible plan move up to at least the Start tier, or at least the Build tier if monthly credits exceed $200. The credits do not count toward moving to a higher tier.
items.value: Linked org gets at least Start tier (Build if credits are over $200/month)
items.short_quote: Organizations linked to an eligible plan move up to at least the Start tier.
items.caveats: Spend caps reset on the 1st of each calendar month, while credits refresh on the billing cycle.

items.claim: API credits are being rolled out over a few days, so some eligible users may not see the offer yet.
items.value: Rolling out (update dated October 7, 2026)
items.short_quote: We’re rolling out API credits over a few days
items.caveats: The FAQ says this is not the Agent SDK credit announced in June, which is not available.

items.topic: Subscription usage via Agent SDK / claude -p
items.claim: When signed in with a Claude plan (not an API key), the Agent SDK and claude -p draw from the subscription's usage limits and do not use API credits. A June 15, 2026 update paused previously announced changes to Agent SDK usage.
items.value: Subscription login draws on plan limits; API key draws on Console credits
items.short_quote: the Claude Agent SDK and claude -p still draw from your subscription limits
items.caveats: This describes how usage is metered, not whether a given use case is permitted. For permission, see the auth-* items.

items.claim: Plan prices shown on claude.com/pricing (as fetched): Pro $20/month billed monthly or $17/month with annual billing ($200 upfront); Max from $100/month, including $100-$200/month in API credits; Team Standard $25/seat billed monthly ($20 annual), Team Premium $125/seat billed monthly ($100 annual). Prices exclude applicable tax.
items.value: Pro $20/mo; Max from $100/mo; Team Standard $25/seat/mo, Premium $125/seat/mo (monthly billing); excl. tax
items.short_quote: Prices shown don’t include applicable tax.
items.caveats: The page was fetched from a US context and showed USD. A visitor in France may see local-currency prices. The page shows Max only as 'From $100', not the Max 20x price.

items.topic: Subscription vs API key in Claude Code
items.claim: If ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is set, Claude Code authenticates with that key instead of the subscription, which produces API charges. In non-interactive (-p) mode the key is always used when present. Max monthly API credits cannot be used in Claude Code.
items.value: API key takes precedence: billed to Console, not to the subscription
items.short_quote: resulting in API usage charges rather than using your subscription's included usage
items.caveats: The -p detail comes from https://code.claude.com/docs/en/authentication.

items.claim: Max and Team monthly API credits were announced in an October 7, 2026 update on the Agent SDK help article.
items.value: Update dated October 7, 2026
items.short_quote: Claude Max and Team plans now include monthly API credits.

items.topic: Subscription login for an automated product
items.claim: The Agent SDK docs say third-party developers may not offer claude.ai login or rate limits for their products, including agents built on the Agent SDK, unless previously approved. They direct developers to API key authentication.
items.value: Use API key auth for Agent SDK products
items.short_quote: Use the API key authentication methods described in the Quickstart instead.
items.caveats: The same note appears in the Agent SDK quickstart (https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/quickstart).

items.topic: Subscription login for an automated product
items.claim: Claude Code's Legal and compliance page says developers building products or services that interact with Claude, including with the Agent SDK, should use API key authentication via the Console or a supported cloud provider.
items.value: Products/services: use API key auth
items.short_quote: should use API key authentication through Claude Console or a supported cloud provider
items.caveats: The page does not specifically address a solo developer's own scheduled job feeding a public website. A public news site is plausibly a 'product or service', which points to API-key auth. That is an interpretation, not an explicit ruling.

items.topic: Subscription login for an automated product
items.claim: OAuth (subscription) authentication is intended exclusively for subscription purchasers and for ordinary use of Claude Code and native Anthropic apps.
items.value: OAuth = ordinary use of Claude Code and native apps only
items.short_quote: designed to support ordinary use of Claude Code and other native Anthropic applications

items.topic: Subscription login for an automated product
items.claim: Advertised Pro and Max usage limits assume ordinary, individual usage of Claude Code and the Agent SDK. Anthropic reserves the right to enforce authentication restrictions without prior notice.
items.value: Limits assume ordinary individual use; enforcement possible without notice
items.short_quote: assume ordinary, individual usage of Claude Code and the Agent SDK
items.caveats: The page says to contact sales with questions about permitted authentication for a use case.

items.claim: The Consumer Terms (which govern Free, Pro and Max) prohibit accessing the Services by automated or non-human means, such as a bot or script, except via an Anthropic API key or where Anthropic explicitly permits it.
items.value: Automated access prohibited unless via API key or explicitly permitted
items.short_quote: through automated or non-human means, whether through a bot, script, or otherwise
items.caveats: Consumer Terms effective Oct 8, 2025 (version shown on the page). Claude Code docs explicitly provide claude -p and setup-token for scripts and CI, which may count as 'explicitly permitted' for ordinary Claude Code use. Server-side automation for a public site is not explicitly permitted anywhere I found.

items.claim: The Commercial Terms govern any Anthropic API key and the Console, while the Consumer Terms govern Claude.ai, Pro and Max. Use of the Agent SDK is governed by the Commercial Terms, including when it powers products offered to end users.
items.value: API key / Console / Agent SDK: Commercial Terms; subscriptions: Consumer Terms
items.short_quote: Commercial Terms of Service govern your use of any Anthropic API key
items.caveats: The Agent SDK statement is on https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/overview. The Claude Code legal page lists Commercial Terms for Team/Enterprise/API and Consumer Terms for Free/Pro/Max.

items.claim: `claude setup-token` generates a one-year OAuth token (CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN) for CI pipelines and scripts where browser login isn't available. It authenticates with the Claude subscription, requires a Pro, Max, Team or Enterprise plan, and can only make model requests.
items.value: One-year OAuth token; requires a paid plan
items.short_quote: For CI pipelines, scripts, or other environments where interactive browser login isn't available
items.caveats: Technical capability does not equal permission for a product. auth-01 to auth-05 still apply. Usage draws on subscription limits, not API credits.

items.claim: Claude Code bare mode (--bare) never reads OAuth credentials and does not read CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN. It requires ANTHROPIC_API_KEY or an apiKeyHelper.
items.value: Bare mode: API key only
items.short_quote: bare mode doesn't use your subscription login

items.claim: The Agent SDK quickstart says to get an API key from the Claude Console and set ANTHROPIC_API_KEY. Bedrock, Vertex, Foundry and Claude Platform on AWS credentials are also supported.
items.value: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the Console
items.short_quote: Get an API key from the Claude Console
items.caveats: The SDK doesn't load .env files automatically (per the quickstart).

items.topic: Free API credits: new Console accounts
items.claim: New API users get a small amount of free credits to test the API. No amount is published.
items.value: Small, unspecified free trial credit
items.short_quote: New users receive a small amount of free credits to test the API.
items.caveats: Claude Academy says the same (https://academy.claude.com/courses/claude-platform-101/your-first-api-call). Amount, expiry and conditions are not stated on any official page I read; the user should check the Console Billing page after sign-up.

items.claim: Promotional (free) credits are offered at Anthropic's sole discretion, for example at sign-up. They expire at the time indicated, or after one year if none is given. All credits are non-refundable and cannot be transferred or sold.
items.value: Discretionary; expiry as indicated or 1 year; non-transferable
items.short_quote: Anthropic may, in its sole discretion, offer Customer free credits
items.caveats: Supplemental Credit Terms effective Mar 4, 2024.

items.claim: The Claude Startups program is closed to new applicants: the current cohort is full (update dated Oct 13, 2026).
items.value: Closed to new applications
items.short_quote: Our current cohort is now full, and we’re not accepting new applications right now.
items.caveats: Existing members keep access.

items.topic: Free API credits: startup program (when open)
items.claim: When open, Claude Startups gave a one-time $1,000 API credit plus a year of Team. Eligibility: startups founded in the last five years or funded in the last two. VC-backed founders in Anthropic's partner network may get up to $100K in extra API credits through their VC. Credits apply only to the first-party API via the Console.
items.value: $1,000 USD one-time API credit (program currently closed)
items.short_quote: Startups founded in the last five years or funded in the last two
items.caveats: The $100K VC figure and the first-party-only restriction come from https://claude.com/programs/startups. A student side project without a company likely would not qualify anyway.

items.claim: The former 'student builders' page now redirects to the Claude Campus program. Undergraduates can apply to lead a Claude Builder Club and receive a USD 3,600 stipend, and clubs share resources such as API credits with members. Applicants must be 18+ with work authorization in their country of study. Applications ran Sept 1-12 and the program is closed for Fall 2026.
items.value: No published individual student API credit; Campus program closed for Fall 2026
items.short_quote: The program is closed for Fall 2026
items.caveats: I found no official per-student API credit amount or open self-serve student credit program. The Education plan on claude.com/pricing mentions 'Dedicated API credits and educational features for student learning', but it is an institution-level plan sold through sales.

items.claim: The AI for Science program gives researchers in academia and nonprofits, working on high-priority scientific topics (focus on biology/life sciences), up to $20,000 in API credits for 6 months. Applications are reviewed on the first Monday of each month.
items.value: Up to $20,000 USD for 6 months (researchers only)
items.short_quote: up to $20,000 in API credits to your account for a 6-month period
items.caveats: A news-curation app is not scientific research, so this is unlikely to apply.

items.claim: The pricing docs say academic and research discounts might be available, and volume discounts are negotiated case by case.
items.value: Possible; negotiated
items.short_quote: Academic and research discounts might be available.
items.caveats: No published criteria or amounts.

items.claim: Claude Opus 5.5 (claude-opus-5-5) prices per million tokens. Cache hits cost 0.05x the base input price.
items.value: Input $4; 5m cache write $5; 1h cache write $8; cache hit $0.20; output $20 (USD / MTok)
items.short_quote: All prices are in USD.
items.caveats: Prices exclude tax (see bill-03). 1M context at standard pricing (no long-context surcharge).

items.claim: Claude Sonnet 5.5 (claude-sonnet-5-5) prices per million tokens. Cache hits cost 0.05x the base input price.
items.value: Input $2; 5m cache write $2.50; 1h cache write $4; cache hit $0.10; output $10 (USD / MTok)
items.caveats: 1M context at standard pricing (no long-context surcharge).

items.topic: API prices: Claude Haiku 5.5 (prompts up to 100K tokens)
items.claim: Claude Haiku 5.5 (claude-haiku-5-5) prices per million tokens for requests whose prompt is 100,000 tokens or fewer.
items.value: Input $0.10; 5m cache write $0.125; 1h cache write $0.20; cache hit $0.01; output $0.50 (USD / MTok)
items.caveats: claude.com/pricing shows the same figures.

items.topic: API prices: Claude Haiku 5.5 long-prompt tier
items.claim: Claude Haiku 5.5 charges higher prices for any request whose prompt exceeds 100,000 tokens. Prompt length counts all input tokens, including cache reads and writes, and each request is priced on its own.
items.value: Over 100K prompt: input $0.50; 5m cache write $0.625; 1h cache write $1; cache hit $0.05; output $2.50 (USD / MTok)
items.short_quote: a request whose prompt is over 100,000 tokens pays higher prices
items.caveats: This is the only long-prompt tier among the three models.

items.topic: API prices: long context for other models
items.claim: Claude 4.6 and later models, except Haiku 5.5, include the full 1M token context window at standard pricing, so Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 have no long-context surcharge.
items.value: Opus 5.5 / Sonnet 5.5: same per-token price up to 1M tokens
items.short_quote: include the full 1M token context window at standard pricing

items.claim: Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 all have a 1M token context window and 128K max output. Opus 5.5 has adaptive thinking always on with default effort medium. Sonnet 5.5 defaults to effort high and Haiku 5.5 to effort medium.
items.value: 1M context, 128K output; IDs claude-opus-5-5, claude-sonnet-5-5, claude-haiku-5-5
items.caveats: I did not verify how thinking tokens are billed (presumably as output). This matters for estimates because thinking is always on for Opus 5.5.

items.claim: Claude 4.7 and later models use a newer tokenizer that produces about 30% more tokens for the same text than earlier models.
items.value: About +30% tokens vs. older models
items.short_quote: This tokenizer produces approximately 30% more tokens for the same text.
items.caveats: The page says the exact increase depends on content. French text was not specifically addressed.

items.claim: US-only inference (inference_geo: 'us') multiplies all token prices by 1.1x, while global routing (the default) uses standard pricing. Fast mode for Opus 5.5 costs $8 input / $40 output per MTok and is not available with the Batch API.
items.value: US-only 1.1x; Opus 5.5 fast mode $8/$40 USD per MTok
items.short_quote: Fast mode is not available with the Batch API
items.caveats: Neither modifier is needed for this project.

items.claim: Using tools adds a tool-use system prompt: 286 tokens for Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 (tool_choice auto/none), plus the tool definitions themselves.
items.value: 286 extra input tokens per request with tools
items.caveats: Haiku 5.5 uses 406 tokens for tool_choice any/tool.

items.claim: The Batch API charges 50% of standard prices on all usage. Batch prices per MTok (input/output): Opus 5.5 $2/$10, Sonnet 5.5 $1/$5, Haiku 5.5 $0.05/$0.25 (prompts up to 100K) or $0.25/$1.25 (over 100K).
items.short_quote: All usage is charged at 50 percent of the standard API prices.
items.caveats: The discount stacks with prompt caching.

items.claim: There is no firm turnaround guarantee. Most batches finish within 1 hour, and results are available when all requests finish or after 24 hours. Batches that don't finish within 24 hours expire, and expired requests are not billed.
items.value: Best effort; most under 1 h; 24 h expiry window
items.short_quote: Batches expire if processing does not complete within 24 hours.
items.caveats: Processing may slow with demand. Fits a pipeline that runs a few times per day.

items.claim: A batch can hold up to 100,000 requests or 256 MB, whichever comes first. Results are available for 29 days. Batches are not eligible for Zero Data Retention.
items.value: 100,000 requests / 256 MB per batch; results kept 29 days
items.short_quote: Batch results are available for 29 days after creation.

items.topic: Message Batches API with caching and web search
items.claim: Within batches, cache hits are best effort (typically 30-98%), and the docs suggest the 1-hour cache for shared context. Web search inside batches is throttled per org. Batch usage does not affect Messages API rate limits.
items.value: Best-effort cache hits; batch usage separate from Messages API limits
items.short_quote: cache hits are provided on a best-effort basis
items.caveats: Start tier Batch limits: 1,000 RPM, 200,000 requests in queue, 100,000 per batch (https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/rate-limits).

items.claim: The minimum cacheable prompt is 512 tokens for Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5. Shorter prompts are processed without caching and no error is returned.
items.value: 512 tokens (Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5)
items.short_quote: 512 tokens for Claude Fable 5.1, Claude Mythos 5.1, Claude Opus 5.5
items.caveats: Check usage.cache_creation_input_tokens / cache_read_input_tokens to confirm caching happened.

items.claim: The default cache lifetime is 5 minutes and is refreshed free on each hit. A 1-hour TTL costs more: writes are 2x base input versus 1.25x for 5 minutes. Up to 4 cache breakpoints are allowed. Cache reads are 0.05x base input for Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 and 0.1x for Haiku 5.5.
items.value: 5 min default; 1 h option; write 1.25x / 2x; read 0.05x (Opus/Sonnet 5.5), 0.1x (Haiku 5.5)
items.short_quote: refreshed for no additional cost each time the cached content is used
items.caveats: Multipliers are from the pricing page.

items.claim: Server-side web search costs $10 per 1,000 searches plus standard token costs. Search results count as input tokens in that turn and later turns. Each search counts as one use regardless of result count, and failed searches are not billed.
items.value: $10 USD per 1,000 searches + tokens
items.short_quote: $10 USD per 1,000 searches
items.caveats: Web search is on by default unless an admin disables it in Console Capabilities, where domains can also be restricted.

items.claim: The server-side web fetch tool has no per-use fee; only tokens for fetched content are billed. A max_content_tokens parameter caps size. The docs estimate an average 10 kB webpage at about 2,500 tokens.
items.value: No per-use fee; tokens only (about 2,500 tokens per 10 kB page)
items.short_quote: The web fetch tool is available on the Claude API at no additional cost.
items.caveats: There is no default max_uses limit, so set one to control cost.

items.claim: Code execution is free when web_search_20260209+ or web_fetch_20260209+ is in the request, as with dynamic filtering. Otherwise each org gets 1,550 free hours per month, then $0.05 per hour per container.
items.value: Free with web search/fetch; else 1,550 free h/month, then $0.05/h/container
items.short_quote: Code execution is free when used with web search or web fetch.
items.caveats: claude.com/pricing states this as 50 free hours daily per organization.

items.claim: Self-serve Console orgs pay with prepaid usage credits bought on the Billing page before using the API. Credits are available immediately, and the API stops when the balance hits zero. Only successful calls are billed, but a request that was on track to succeed is still charged if the client disconnects.
items.value: Prepaid credits (default)
items.short_quote: Buy credits before you use the API
items.caveats: The pricing doc separately says 'Billing is based on actual monthly usage' and 'Credit card and invoicing options are available'. The support article is clearer that prepaid is the self-serve default.

items.topic: Console billing: credit expiry and refunds
items.claim: Purchased credits expire one year from the purchase date, the expiry cannot be extended, and all credit purchases are non-refundable.
items.value: 1-year expiry; non-refundable
items.short_quote: Credits expire one year from the purchase date

items.claim: Auto-reload is optional and buys credits when the balance falls below a threshold the user sets, topping up to a target. Charges are made plus applicable taxes, so API prices exclude tax. Tax is calculated from the billing address, which for self-serve API accounts comes from the payment method.
items.value: Optional auto-reload; taxes added on top of the USD prices
items.short_quote: plus applicable taxes
items.caveats: The billing-address rule is from https://support.claude.com/en/articles/12997130-understanding-your-billing-address-and-tax-calculation. I found no official statement of the VAT rate for a French individual. Leaving auto-reload off keeps a hard stop.

items.claim: Monthly invoicing in arrears (a Stripe invoice at month end) is only for orgs with an invoicing arrangement set up through Sales. It is not self-serve.
items.value: Invoicing via Sales only
items.short_quote: Console organizations with an invoicing arrangement set up through our Sales team
items.caveats: Invoices below $0.50 aren't charged on their own and roll forward (https://support.claude.com/en/articles/16608069-understanding-your-claude-api-invoices).

items.claim: No official page I read states a minimum credit purchase amount. The help article only says to enter the amount to buy.
items.value: Not documented
items.short_quote: Enter the amount of credits you want to purchase and confirm.
items.caveats: Check the Buy credits dialog at platform.claude.com/settings/billing. Do not assume a figure.

items.claim: Standard accounts pay by major credit card, and all payments are in USD. Onboarding asks for organization and use-case details before payment. After buying credits the API can be used in a commercial application, under the Commercial Terms.
items.value: Credit card; USD
items.short_quote: Major credit cards are accepted for standard accounts.
items.caveats: Onboarding details are from https://support.claude.com/en/articles/8114531-i-created-a-claude-console-organization-how-do-i-start-using-the-claude-api.

items.claim: Each tier has a monthly spend cap: Start $500, Build $1,000, Scale $200,000 per calendar month. When the cap is reached, API usage pauses until 00:00 UTC on the 1st of the next month and returns HTTP 429 enforced_spend_limit_reached.
items.value: Start $500 USD; Build $1,000 USD; Scale $200,000 USD per month
items.short_quote: Each of the Start, Build, and Scale tiers carries a monthly spend cap

items.claim: Users can set their own monthly spend limit below the tier cap on the Billing page. When it is reached, requests return HTTP 400 invalid_request_error until the limit is raised or access resumes. Workspaces can have their own spend and rate limits, but not the default Workspace.
items.value: Custom org spend limit yes; workspace limits yes (not on the default workspace)
items.short_quote: set your own spend limit below your tier’s cap to control costs
items.caveats: Lets the user enforce whatever monthly budget he chooses.

items.claim: Usage tiers are assigned automatically from usage history and account standing, and no deposit or purchase moves an org up. New orgs may start in an Evaluation tier with limits below the standard Start limits. Higher limits can be requested once the org uses at least 50% of current limits.
items.value: No deposit requirement; automatic; possible Evaluation tier at start
items.short_quote: There's no deposit or purchase that moves you up
items.caveats: Evaluation tier detail is from https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/rate-limits. Evaluation tier limits and spend cap are not published.

items.claim: Start tier Messages API limits for Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5, each with its own bucket. For these models only uncached input tokens count toward ITPM.
items.short_quote: only uncached input tokens count toward your ITPM rate limits
items.caveats: Far above what 1-5 publications/day needs. Build tier: 5,000 RPM / 5M ITPM / 1M OTPM.

open_questions: Which Claude plan does the user actually have (Free, Pro, Max 5x/20x or Team)? Only Max and Team include monthly API credits ($100 / $200 / up to $500 pooled). Pro includes none.

If he is on Max or Team, does the 'API credits' section already appear in claude.ai Settings > Billing? The rollout announced Oct 7, 2026 was 'over a few days', and claiming requires 7 days on the plan.
How large is the free trial credit for a new Console account, and when does it expire? Official docs only say 'a small amount'.
Is there a minimum credit purchase in the Console? No official page states one; check the Buy credits dialog.
What VAT or tax rate applies to a French individual buying API credits? Official pages only say prices exclude tax and that the billing address determines tax.
What are the Evaluation tier limits and spend cap for brand-new orgs? Not published.
How are adaptive-thinking tokens billed (presumably as output tokens)? I did not verify this, and it matters for Opus 5.5, where thinking is always on.

Does Anthropic permit a solo developer's server-side scheduled job feeding a public website to run on subscription OAuth (setup-token)? No explicit permission was found. Docs say products and services should use API keys, and the Consumer Terms bar automated access except via API key. Treat API key auth as the compliant path, or ask Anthropic sales/support.

Do the Max/Team monthly API credits cover server-tool fees such as web search ($10 per 1,000 searches)? The credits article lists the Claude API generally but does not mention server tools explicitly.
Does claude.com/pricing show EUR prices to visitors in France? The fetched page showed USD.

verdicts.note: The page says the Pro plan does not include API usage through the Claude Console, and that Console access is needed to pay for API usage separately. It also says Pro is $20/month in the US, shown in local currency where supported, with tax included or added at checkout. Page is marked 'Updated over 2 weeks ago'.
Confirmed on both points: the article says 'the Claude API is billed separately', and it also says Max and Team plans include monthly credits for the Claude API.

Both the platform doc and help article 17154008 list Max 5x, Max 20x and Team (discounted Team plans included) as eligible, and say Free, Pro and Enterprise plans aren't eligible. Neither page carries a calendar date. The October 7, 2026 date appears only on help article 15036540.

research.dimension: Hosting for a mostly-TypeScript stack (Next.js web app + Node worker + Postgres/SQLite-compatible DB + scheduler): Vercel, Netlify, Cloudflare Workers/D1, Neon, Supabase, Turso. Free-tier limits, first paid tier, and restrictions relevant to CURATION AI (checked 2026-10-30 on official pages)

items.claim: The Vercel Hobby plan is restricted to non-commercial personal use. All commercial use requires Pro or Enterprise.
items.value: Hobby = $0, personal non-commercial only
items.short_quote: Hobby teams are restricted to non-commercial personal use only.
items.caveats: The pricing page says the same thing: Hobby is 'for personal, non-commercial use'.

items.topic: Vercel Hobby - what counts as commercial
items.claim: Vercel treats a deployment as commercial if anyone involved in producing it makes money from it. Examples include taking payments from visitors, advertising a product or service for sale, being paid to build or host the site, a site whose main purpose is affiliate linking, and showing ads such as Google AdSense. Asking for donations is not commercial.
items.value: Ads, affiliate-first sites, paid work and payments are commercial; donations are not
items.short_quote: The inclusion of advertisements, including but not limited to online advertising platforms
items.caveats: If CURATION AI ever shows ads, earns affiliate revenue or charges users, Hobby is no longer allowed. A purely personal or student prototype without monetization looks eligible. Vercel says to contact Support if you are unsure.

items.claim: Each month, Hobby includes 1,000,000 function invocations, 4 CPU-hours of Active CPU, 360 GB-hours of provisioned memory, 100 GB of Fast Data Transfer, 10 GB of Fast Origin Transfer, 1,000,000 CDN requests, 5,000 image transformations, 50,000 Web Analytics events and 50,000 Workflow events.
items.value: 1M invocations / 4 CPU-hrs / 360 GB-hrs / 100 GB transfer per month, $0
items.short_quote: 4 CPU-hrs
items.caveats: These are per-month allotments. Hobby users can't buy extra usage (per https://vercel.com/pricing).

items.claim: In most cases, a Hobby team that goes over a usage limit has to wait 30 days before using that feature again. Hobby users can't buy additional usage.
items.value: Feature blocked for up to 30 days once the cap is exceeded
items.short_quote: you will have to wait until 30 days have passed
items.caveats: Some features have shorter pause periods; Web Analytics, for example, resumes after 7 days.

items.claim: On Hobby, each cron job can run at most once per day. Any cron expression that would run more often, such as hourly or every 30 minutes, fails at deployment. Timing precision is per hour (±59 min). Each project can have up to 100 cron jobs.
items.value: Hobby: 100 cron jobs/project, minimum interval once per day, ±59 min precision
items.short_quote: will trigger anywhere between 1:00 am and 1:59 am
items.caveats: This matters for CURATION AI: collecting 'a few times per day' is not possible with Vercel Cron on Hobby. The options are one daily run on Hobby, Pro, or an external scheduler triggering an endpoint (external schedulers were not researched here).

items.claim: On Pro and Enterprise, cron jobs can run as often as once per minute, with per-minute precision, up to 100 cron jobs per project.
items.value: Pro: minimum interval 1 minute, per-minute precision
items.short_quote: Once per minute
items.caveats: Cron jobs are included in all plans, but each run invokes a Vercel Function, so normal function usage and pricing apply.

items.claim: With Fluid compute (Node.js/Bun/Python), Hobby functions have a 300 s default and a 300 s maximum. Pro and Enterprise have a 300 s default, an 800 s maximum, and an extended maximum of 1800 s (30 min) in beta.
items.value: Hobby 300 s max; Pro 800 s max (1800 s beta)
items.short_quote: Hobby: 300s default and maximum.
items.caveats: A function that times out returns 504 FUNCTION_INVOCATION_TIMEOUT. The worker must collect and make its LLM calls within 5 minutes per invocation on Hobby, or split the work across several invocations.

items.claim: Hobby functions get 2 GB / 1 vCPU, with no option to raise it. Pro and Enterprise default to 2 GB / 1 vCPU and can go up to 4 GB / 2 vCPU.
items.value: Hobby 2 GB; Pro up to 4 GB
items.short_quote: Hobby: 2 GB, Pro and Ent: 4 GB
items.caveats: The request or response payload limit is 4.5 MB on all plans.

items.topic: Vercel - Active CPU excludes I/O wait
items.claim: Active CPU only counts time the code is actually computing. Time spent waiting on I/O, such as AI model calls or database queries, is not counted. This matters for LLM-calling jobs.
items.value: I/O wait not billed as Active CPU
items.short_quote: Waiting for I/O (e.g. calling AI models, database queries) does not count
items.caveats: Provisioned memory time is still metered while the instance runs: 360 GB-hrs included on Hobby, from $0.0106/GB-hr on Pro.

The definition and all five examples match: payments, advertising a product or service for sale, being paid to build or host, affiliate-first sites, and ads such as AdSense. Donations are explicitly not commercial. The page says to contact Support if unsure. The definition also covers a paid employee or consultant writing the code.

The Hobby table lists all the stated figures: 1M invocations, 4 CPU-hrs Active CPU, 360 GB-hrs, 100 GB Fast Data Transfer, 10 GB Fast Origin Transfer, 1M CDN requests, 5,000 image transformations, 50,000 Web Analytics events and 50,000 Workflow events per month. vercel.com/pricing says Hobby users 'cannot purchase additional usage'.
The 'Hobby billing cycle' section has both the 30-day wait (said to apply 'in most cases') and the 7-day Web Analytics exception. The no-extra-purchase rule is on https://vercel.com/pricing.

Pro and Enterprise: once per minute, per-minute precision, 100 jobs per project. The page says cron jobs are included in all plans and invoke Functions, so function pricing applies.

With Fluid compute (Node.js/Bun/Python): Hobby 300 s default and maximum; Pro/Enterprise 300 s default, 800 s max, 1800 s extended max in beta. A timeout returns 504 FUNCTION_INVOCATION_TIMEOUT. /docs/plans/hobby shows the same figures.
Hobby: 2 GB / 1 vCPU default and max. Pro/Ent: 2 GB / 1 vCPU default, up to 4 GB / 2 vCPU. Request/response body limit is 4.5 MB (413 FUNCTION_PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE).

The 'Cost and usage' section says I/O wait, such as calling AI models or database queries, does not count toward active CPU. Provisioned memory is billed on allocated memory times running time. The Pro rate 'Starting at $0.0106 per GB-hr' is on the fair-use page.
Domains per Project: Hobby 50, Pro Unlimited*. The footnote gives a soft limit of 100,000 per project on Pro, raisable on request. The /docs/plans/hobby comparison table also shows 50 vs Unlimited.

Projects 200, Deployments Created per Day 100 (Pro 6000), 'Concurrent Deployments' 1 on Hobby (the item calls it concurrent builds), runtime logs 1 hour on Hobby and 1 day on Pro. open_questions: GitHub only documents the 60-day inactivity auto-disable for public repositories. Whether scheduled workflows in private repositories are ever auto-disabled is not stated.
GitHub does not quantify its scheduled-workflow delays and offers no SLA. Real-world delay and drop rates would need observation.
Render, Railway and the Fly.io docs page do not say whether VAT is included. For a French individual, EU VAT may be added at checkout. Only fly.io/pricing says its prices exclude tax.
Render's pricing page lists custom domains as a Hobby workspace feature, but this run did not confirm that a Free web service (not only paid ones) can use a custom domain.
The Railway cron docs do not confirm that a cron-scheduled service is billed only while running. That is inferred from the per-second billing statement.
Fly.io does not state a per-second price for shared-cpu-1x in its docs. The pricing-page column reading USD 0.0030 is assumed to be hourly.
The Hetzner shared-vCPU plans were labelled 'not available' on 2026-10-30. It is unknown whether this is temporary or applies to every location, and the cost of backups and snapshots was not checked.

Google Cloud Run's free tier needs a billing account with a card. Artifact Registry and Cloud Build free-tier limits for hosting the container image were not checked, and they can cause small charges.
PythonAnywhere's pricing page uses '$' without naming the currency, does not state VAT, and does not show the price of the Postgres add-on on Custom plans.

Free managed Postgres options other than Render (which expires after 30 days), such as Neon, Supabase or Turso, were outside this dimension. They may be needed for a durable run-trace DB on a zero budget.

verdicts.note: The page says the use of standard GitHub-hosted runners is free in public repositories (also for GitHub Pages and Dependabot). It lists this usage as staying free without reducing the included compute usage. Larger runners are billed for public repositories.

The plans page (docs.github.com/en/get-started/learning-about-github/githubs-plans) states '$12 USD of included compute usage per month' for Free and 500 MB of Packages storage. It does not give artifact or cache figures. The billing page gives them: Free has 500 MB artifact storage, $12 USD and 10 GB cache per repository; Pro has 1 GB and $18 USD. It also says artifact storage is shared with GitHub Packages, the cache is a separate allowance, and included compute resets at the start of each billing cycle.

The Free plan shows '2,000 CI/CD minutes/month' and 'Free for public repositories', with 500MB of Packages storage. The USD 12 / 0.006 equivalence is the researcher's own calculation. The billing docs give a minutes equivalent only for Enterprise Cloud.
Per-minute rates: Linux 1-core x64 $0.002, Linux 2-core x64 $0.006, Windows 2-core $0.010, macOS 3/4-core $0.062. Prices are in USD, and the page makes no VAT or tax statement.

Quoted verbatim: without a valid payment method, 'usage is blocked once you consume the included compute usage.' The 90% and 100% email notifications and budgets are both mentioned. Larger runners require a valid payment method.

Confirmed verbatim: 'The shortest interval you can run scheduled workflows is once every 5 minutes.' Schedules default to UTC, and an optional IANA timezone string is supported. They run on the latest commit on the default branch, and only if the workflow file is on the default branch.

The note says the schedule event can be delayed during high loads, including 'the start of every hour'. GitHub advises scheduling at a different time of the hour. No SLA and no maximum delay are documented.
Verbatim: 'If the load is sufficiently high enough, some queued jobs may be dropped.'

Both this page and the events page say: 'In a public repository, scheduled workflows are automatically disabled when no repository activity has occurred in 60 days.' Neither page says anything about private repos. Re-enabling uses the standard Enable workflow button or `gh workflow enable`.

Job execution time is 6 hours: 'If a job reaches this limit, the job is terminated and fails.' A workflow run can last 35 days, including waiting and approval time, and is cancelled at the limit. GitHub Free allows 20 concurrent jobs on standard hosted runners (5 macOS max).

The full sentence is 'With the exception of single-CPU runners, each GitHub-hosted runner is a new virtual machine (VM) hosted by GitHub.' Single-CPU runners are in a container on a shared VM. The page does not explicitly state that nothing persists between jobs, so that remains an inference.

Plans: Hobby $0/mo + compute, Pro $25/mo + compute, Scale $499/mo + compute, Enterprise custom. Hobby allows up to 25 services and includes 5 GB of bandwidth, then $0.15/GB (Pro 25 GB, Scale 1 TB). The 'Custom domains' claim needs a qualifier: Hobby includes 2 custom domains, then $0.25/domain/month (Pro 15, Scale 25). The FAQ says the Pro/Scale fee is waived for a month with no services and no activity. The page makes no tax or VAT statement.

Verbatim: Render spins down a Free web service 'that goes 15 minutes without receiving any inbound traffic', including HTTP requests and WebSocket messages. Spinning back up 'takes about one minute', and a loading page is shown meanwhile. Render may restart Free services at any time.

Each workspace gets 750 Free instance hours per calendar month. Spun-down services do not consume hours, and unused hours do not roll over. When the hours run out, all Free web services are suspended until the next month. Free web services have no persistent disks, no edge caching, no one-off jobs, no shell and no scaling. The filesystem is ephemeral, and ports 25, 465 and 587 are blocked. They also cannot receive private network traffic. The 0.1 CPU / 512 MB size is confirmed on render.com/docs/compute-plans and render.com/pricing.

Verbatim: 'Other service types don't support Free instances.' The service types that do are Static Site, Web Service, Postgres and Key Value. The compute-plans page says private services and background workers use the same tiers without the free plan, and the smallest is 0.5c-512mb.

Cron Jobs table: 0.5c-512mb (less than 1 CPU, 512 MB) costs $0.00016/minute; 1c-2g costs $0.00058/minute. Billing is 'Prorated by the second'. The August 2026 renaming of 'starter' to 0.5c-512mb is confirmed on render.com/docs/compute-plans. The page makes no VAT statement.
Verbatim: 'There is a minimum monthly charge of $1 per cron job service.' Billing is prorated by the second on active running time.
Verbatim: 'Render stops an active run after 12 hours.' The page recommends a workflow or background worker for longer tasks.

The single-run guarantee, delay-until-finish behaviour, UTC, and cancellation on manual trigger are all confirmed. One detail is wrong: the page has no 5-minute example. Its examples are every ten minutes (*/10), daily at noon UTC, and every 60 minutes Mon-Fri. No minimum interval is stated.
verdicts.corrected_value: No overlapping runs (the next scheduled run waits for the active one); UTC; no documented minimum interval; the doc's examples use 10-minute, 60-minute and daily schedules (none at 5 minutes)

verdicts.note: Services & Workers table: 'Less than 1 CPU $7/month 512 MB RAM 0.5c-512mb'. SSDs (persistent disks) cost $0.25/GB per month. The FAQ says compute is prorated to the second. The page makes no VAT statement.

Free Postgres: one per workspace, a fixed 1 GB of storage, expiry 30 days after creation, and a 14-day grace period to upgrade before deletion. An expired database is inaccessible unless upgraded, and Free databases have no backups. The pricing page lists Free Postgres at $0/month with 256 MB RAM and 100 connections.

Postgres table: 'Less than 1 CPU $6/month 256 MB RAM 100 connections 0.1c-256mb'. The page also lists expandable storage at $0.30/GB and '1 GB SSD storage included'. The Hobby point-in-time recovery window is 3 days (7 on Pro and above). The page makes no VAT statement.

Verbatim: Free Key Value instances 'do not continually persist their state to disk', so all data is lost on restart. Only one is allowed per workspace, and data is lost on upgrade. Pricing page: Free has 25 MB RAM and 50 connections; the smallest paid plan is $10/month (256 MB RAM, 256 MB storage, 200 connections).

The page says 'Deploy websites for free, forever' and 'Static Sites Always free to deploy', with custom domains and managed TLS. Hobby includes a standard build pipeline of 500 mins per month, then $5 per 1K mins. render.com/docs/free confirms that static sites count against included bandwidth and pipeline minutes.

The short quote is verbatim on docs.railway.com/reference/pricing/plans, not on railway.com/pricing. railway.com/pricing shows: Free $0 per month (30-day trial with $5 of credits, then $1 per month); Hobby '$5 minimum usage' including $5 of monthly usage credits; Pro '$20 minimum usage' including $20 of credits. The plans doc says usage beyond the included amount is charged as the delta. Neither page makes a VAT statement.

Confirmed: a one-time $5 grant for up to 30 days, after which the account reverts to the Free plan ($1/month, no rollover). Limited Trial has restricted outbound network access; connecting GitHub verifies the account for full access. One wording fix: the doc says Railway deletes stateful volumes 'created by Trial accounts' 30 days after the credits expire. It says nothing about Free-plan volumes.

Per-service limits table: Trial 2 replicas, 1 GB RAM, 2 vCPU, 0.5 GB volume; Free 1 replica, 0.5 GB, 1 vCPU, 0.5 GB; Hobby 6 replicas, 48 GB, 48 vCPU, 5 GB; Pro 42 replicas, 1 TB, 1,000 vCPU, 1 TB. The railway.com/pricing card instead says Hobby allows up to 5 replicas at 8 vCPU / 8 GB each, so the two pages disagree on Hobby replicas.

Rates are verbatim: Memory $0.00000386 per GB/sec, CPU $0.00000772 per vCPU/sec, Volumes $0.00000006 per GB/sec, Egress $0.05 per GB. The plans doc gives about $10/GB-mo, $20/vCPU-mo and $0.15/GB-mo. The quote 'billing is always per-second' was not found on either page. The pricing page headline says 'Pay only for what your app uses, by the second', and the plans doc lists per-minute equivalents. 'Stopped services cost nothing' was not found as a statement. The plans FAQ says the Hobby $5 fee is always paid even if usage is lower.

Verbatim: 'Scheduled runs must be at least 5 minutes apart in UTC.' A new run is skipped if the previous one is still Active. Execution times 'can vary by a few minutes'. The service must exit when done. The doc says Railway 'does not automatically terminate deployments', so no maximum run duration is enforced.

Verbatim: a service 'sleeps somewhere between 5 and 10 minutes after its last outbound traffic.' The first request wakes it with a cold boot and 'may return a 502 Bad Gateway'. The page only says Serverless 'may reduce the usage cost', with no exact billing. Slept services still hold an infrastructure slot and are de-prioritized.

Verbatim: 'New organizations don't have a free tier or a monthly free usage allowance.' Still free after the trial: the first 10GB of snapshots per month, the first 10 single-hostname SSL certificates, inbound data, shared IPv4 and IPv6. Organizations on plans discontinued in October 2024 keep their allowances.

The trial lasts 'up to 2 hours of Machine runtime or 7 days, whichever comes first.' No credit card is needed to start, but one is required afterwards. The same page also says 'All organizations (except for Linked Organizations) require a credit card on file.'

The Machines table shows 'shared-cpu-1x · 256MB $0.0030 $2.19' under Per hour / Per month, billed by the second while running. The docs say the cheapest always-on app is this preset in Ashburn (iad) or Secaucus (ewr), at $2.19 per 30 days. The caveat that prices exclude tax is not supported: no tax statement appears on fly.io/pricing or docs.fly.io/about/pricing, and the docs only say 'Prices are in USD.'

Confirmed: a stopped or suspended Machine costs $0.15/GB/month of rootfs only. Volumes cost $0.15/GB/month on provisioned capacity, including when detached. A dedicated IPv4 costs $2/month. Outbound data costs $0.02/GB in North America and Europe; inbound is free. The docs mention no minimum bill and say there is no monthly platform fee.
Managed Postgres Basic (shared-2x · 1GB) costs $38 per month, and database storage costs $0.28 per GB. The 'excluding tax' caveat is not stated on the page.

Machines can be told to start hourly, daily, weekly or monthly, with 'just interval buckets'. The page lists Cron Manager, Supercronic, in-app schedulers, and external triggers such as GitHub Actions schedule or easycron.

Jobs free tier, based on us-central1 pricing: the first 240,000 vCPU-seconds and 450,000 GiB-seconds free per month. It is aggregated across projects by billing account, resets monthly, and is applied as a spending-based discount using Tier 1 pricing.

Jobs Default (USD): CPU $0.000018 per vCPU-second, memory $0.000002 per GiB-second, rounded up to the nearest 100 ms. In the worked example 5, the job runs in europe-west1, hourly (730 runs/month), 1 minute each, with 1 vCPU and 512 MiB. It costs $0.00, versus $0.45 without the free tier.

Request-based services: 180,000 vCPU-s, 360,000 GiB-s and 2 million requests free per month. Instance-based services: 240,000 vCPU-s and 450,000 GiB-s. Outbound data: 1 GiB free per month within North America. Cloud Build and Artifact Registry pricing is separate and can apply even inside the Cloud Run free tier.

Verbatim: 'By default, each task runs for a maximum of 10 minutes.' The limit can be raised to 168 hours (7 days), or 1 hour with GPUs. The page also says there is no explicit timeout for a job execution. The quotas page calls the filesystem a writable, in-memory filesystem limited by instance memory.

The original URL now 301-redirects to docs.cloud.google.com. Confirmed: '$300 Welcome credit to spend over 90 days'. Without an upgrade, the Free Trial billing account closes and resources stop, followed by a 30-day grace period before permanent deletion. The credit 'can't pay for Gemini API in AI Studio costs', and the Free Tier remains after upgrade. A credit card or payment method is required at signup.
Verbatim: 'Each Google billing account gets 3 jobs per month free.' The free tier is measured at the account level, not per project. A paused job still counts as a job.
A job is billed '$0.10/job/31 days', which is $0.003 per day, calculated per day. Jobs are not billed per execution. The pricing table is in USD.

The page uses the unix-cron string format, and its text reads '* * * * * : the job runs every minute'. The examples table also lists 'Every minute'. The default time zone is UTC, and no minimum interval is stated.

Beginner is $0/month: one web app at your-username.pythonanywhere.com, up to 2 consoles, 100 CPU-seconds, 512MB of storage. External internet is limited to 'Specific sites via HTTP(S) only'. The HTML comparison table marks SSH, scheduled tasks, always-on tasks and MySQL as 'No' for the free column.

The warning is verbatim: scheduled tasks only work in paid accounts or free accounts created before 2026-01-15 (2026-01-08 in the EU). Older free accounts get one daily task that can run for up to two hours.

The page lists '1 web app with 1 web worker and 1 month expiry' as a feature of free accounts in general, not only post-cutoff ones. Older accounts additionally get MySQL and 1 daily scheduled task. The page does not explain how renewal works.

Developer is $10/month: one web app on a custom domain or pythonanywhere.com, 20 hourly or daily scheduled tasks, 1 always-on task, 5,000 CPU-seconds, 5GB, MySQL and SSH. The page also says: 'we give you 2 months free per year, so you only pay for 10 months', plus a 30-day money-back guarantee. Custom costs $10 to $500/month and has an optional Postgres server. The 12-hour per-task limit is confirmed on the ScheduledTasks help page. No currency code or VAT statement appears.

CX23: 2 Intel/AMD vCPU, 4 GB, 40 GB NVMe, '€ 5.99 per month, excl. VAT', € 0.0096 per hour excl. VAT. It includes 20 TB of traffic, is offered in eu-central NBG1/HEL1, and the price includes IPv4. CAX11 costs € 6.49/month excl. VAT. The card carries a 'not available' badge.

Only the Cost-Optimized plans carry a 'not available' badge (all 8: CX23-CX53, CAX11-CAX41). The main cloud page shows 'Currently not available' on the Cost-Optimized block only. Regular Performance plans have no such badge, and CPX02 is labelled 'New'. The tooltip text 'This product is currently unavailable' is in the static HTML of every plan, including all 6 dedicated General Purpose plans. It is probably a template string toggled by JavaScript, so it does not prove a plan is unavailable.
verdicts.corrected_value: On 2026-10-30, Cost-Optimized (CX/CAX) plans were badged 'not available'. Regular Performance (CPX) plans were not badged, and their availability could not be determined from static HTML.

verdicts.note: CPX02 (labelled 'New'): 1 AMD vCPU, 1 GB, 20 GB NVMe, '€ 6.49 per month, excl. VAT', € 0.0104 per hour. It includes 20 TB in FSN1/NBG1/HEL1. The page says the bill 'will never exceed its monthly price cap'. In the US (HIL1/ASH1), CPX11 (2 vCPU, 2 GB, 40 GB) costs € 17.99/month excl. VAT with 1 TB of traffic.
Verbatim: 'Our cloud servers are available to you in Germany, Finland, Singapore, and the USA.' Data centers are in Falkenstein, Nuremberg and Helsinki, with US locations in Hillsboro and Ashburn.
